title: Short direct verdict negations (AITA judgments)
description: This latent fires on brief, formulaic negative-verdict phrases that open or stand alone as a direct judgment, especially in 'Am I the Asshole'-style responses: short exclamations or clauses like 'Not entirely.', 'Not really.', 'No, you're not the asshole.', 'Absolutely not!'. It activates most strongly on terse, syntactically minimal denial/negation statements (often just 2-6 words, frequently starting with 'No' or 'Not') that deliver a clear-cut ruling before or instead of elaboration. It does not activate strongly on longer explanatory or hedging sentences that discuss reasoning, context, or nuance (e.g. 'it's not necessarily about whether you should have...') even if they contain similar words like 'not' or 'asshole', nor on sentences that pose questions, give advice, or list suggestions rather than issuing a direct short verdict.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens that begin items in an enumerated list (e.g. '2.', '3. **', '4.'), particularly in advice-giving or point-by-point breakdown contexts like 'Let's break it down: 1.' or 'Here's why: 1.'. It activates most strongly on the bare digit-plus-period token itself, regardless of what content follows, and appears in both top and mid-strength contexts whenever a response is structured as a numbered list. It would not activate on prose sentences lacking explicit list numbering, even if they discuss similar advice-column or reasoning content, nor on bullet points or lists that use non-numeric markers.

title: Recommending seeking support from others
description: This latent fires on the specific advice-giving pattern of telling someone to reach out to friends, family, a therapist, or other support figures for emotional help or guidance, especially in the templated 'Seek support: Talk to/Reach out to...' phrasing common in advice-list responses. It activates most strongly on the exact bolded header phrases like 'Seek support**:' followed by a recommendation to talk to trusted friends, family members, or mental health professionals, and more weakly on looser paraphrases of the same suggestion embedded in longer sentences. It does not activate on general expressions of sympathy or solidarity ('I'm here to listen', 'you're not alone'), on advice to seek other non-interpersonal resources (financial advisors, savings accounts, apps, classes), or on descriptions of relationship problems/conflict that don't explicitly recommend reaching out to someone for support.

title: Prior agreement or commitment recap
description: This latent fires on statements that recap a factual sequence of agreeing to, committing to, requesting, or fulfilling (or declining) a specific prior arrangement between two parties—e.g. 'You agreed to X and did Y,' 'He asked and you agreed/complied,' 'You had already committed/planned in advance.' These are neutral, third-person recaps of who asked/offered/agreed/paid/showed up, often used to establish the factual timeline of a dispute (as in AITA-style narratives) rather than to evaluate or moralize about it. It does not activate on evaluative, advice-giving, or emotionally validating statements that lack a concrete agreement/commitment structure (e.g. 'It's understandable that you're upset,' 'You should communicate more openly'), nor on general behavioral commentary without a specific ask-agree-fulfill pattern.

title: Benefit-framing 'This can/will help' template
description: This latent fires on the specific sentence-initial construction 'This can/will help [you]...' used to introduce the benefit or positive outcome of a suggested action, especially in advice-giving contexts about building confidence, rapport, connection, trust, or momentum. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic instances of this exact template, particularly when followed by relational/emotional benefits (feel more comfortable, build trust, boost confidence). It activates more weakly but still fires on other sentences elsewhere in advice text that describe similar benefits ('this can help repair relationships', 'this can help him feel heard') even without the exact leading phrase. It does NOT activate on sentences that give advice through other syntactic forms (imperatives, conditionals, 'you might want to', 'by doing X you can...') or that discuss relationship/communication topics without using the 'this can/will help' benefit-statement construction, and it is distinct from latents tracking the topical content (trust, rapport, communication) itself rather than this particular framing device.

title: Validating self-care and boundary-setting
description: This latent fires on second-person affirmations that validate the reader's right to prioritize their own needs, well-being, happiness, or boundaries, typically framed with 'you deserve,' 'you have the right to,' or 'you're taking care of yourself/prioritizing.' It activates most strongly on short, formulaic reassurance statements that directly assert entitlement to self-care or self-prioritization, often as a standalone sentence in advice-column style text. It activates less strongly (in the random sample) on sentences that discuss self-care or boundaries as part of a longer explanatory or advisory context rather than delivering a direct validating affirmation. It would not activate on sentences describing others' actions, general advice about relationships, or factual/explanatory statements that don't center on affirming the reader's own worth or right to self-prioritization.

title: Empathetic conversational opener stock phrase
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic empathy/validation phrases that an assistant uses to open or punctuate a supportive response, such as 'I'm happy to help!', 'I completely understand!', 'I'm so glad you reached out!', and 'I totally understand your concerns!'. It activates most strongly on these exact templated exclamations, especially when they appear as standalone sentences, and more weakly on longer sentences that embed similar validating sentiment ('I understand your concerns and hesitation...', 'It's understandable that...'). It does not activate on substantive advice-giving, situational analysis, or judgment statements (e.g. 'You are not the asshole', 'Here are some thoughts to consider') that lack this stock empathetic-phrase form, even though such sentences share the same supportive-conversation topic.

title: Listing suggested activities or options
description: This latent fires on list items or clauses that enumerate concrete example activities, hobbies, side-hustles, or event types—typically phrased as 'X, Y, or Z' groupings under a bolded category header (e.g., 'Classes or Workshops: cooking, language, art') or as 'This could be a book club, sports team, hiking group...'. It activates strongly on generic advice-style bullet points suggesting things to do, try, join, or sell, especially when framed as interchangeable options connected by 'or'. It does not activate on sentences giving emotional support, asking reflective questions, offering relationship/communication advice, or making single specific recommendations without an enumerated list of alternatives—i.e., prose that reasons about a situation rather than itemizing a menu of options.

title: Token 'Don' detection
description: This latent appears to activate on the specific token or word fragment 'Don', which could represent either the start of a proper name (e.g., 'Don' as in Donald) or the beginning of a contraction like 'Don't'. Given the extremely limited sample (a single truncated sentence), the latent seems tied to this exact surface token rather than to any broader semantic or syntactic pattern. It would not activate on sentences that discuss related concepts (denial, negation, or names) without containing this exact token, nor on other contractions or names that don't share this specific letter sequence. Because only one truncated example is available, the precise contextual conditions (e.g., sentence position, capitalization) that trigger this latent cannot be fully determined.

title: Intro phrase launching a numbered list
description: This latent fires on short transitional lead-in phrases (e.g. 'Here are some points to consider:', 'Here's why:', 'Here are some suggestions:') that immediately precede a numbered or bulleted list, especially at the '1.' marker itself. It activates most strongly on the boilerplate colon-terminated header plus the start of enumeration, regardless of the advice topic that follows. It generalizes somewhat to other list-introducing constructions ('Now, let's examine the situation:', 'To address these concerns, consider the following:') as long as they set up an itemized list. It does not activate on the actual content/advice inside the list items, nor on declarative or opinion sentences that lack this list-launching, colon-plus-enumeration structure (e.g. 'I think you handled it fairly well' or 'However, it's essential to approach the conversation with empathy').

title: Active-listening advice imperatives
description: This latent fires on short imperative-style directives instructing someone to listen actively, show genuine interest/empathy, or avoid interrupting/being defensive — the stock phrasing used in interpersonal-communication advice lists (e.g., 'Listen actively and respond with empathy,' 'Avoid interrupting or offering unsolicited advice'). It activates most strongly on terse, formulaic bullet-point commands built around the core verbs 'listen,' 'ask,' 'show interest/empathy,' and 'avoid interrupting/defensiveness,' often in numbered or bolded advice-list formats. It activates more weakly but still fires on related advice sentences embedded in longer prose about communication, empathy, or conflict resolution. It does NOT activate (or activates only weakly) on sentences that discuss the same relational/communication topics narratively or descriptively — e.g., recounting what someone did, explaining consequences, expressing feelings, or giving advice on unrelated logistics — since the latent tracks the specific imperative 'listen/engage attentively' instruction pattern rather than the general theme of communication or empathy.

title: Self-care advice list items
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic imperative bullet-point recommendations for emotional self-care and stress management, typically phrased as bolded headers like 'Practice mindfulness', 'Take deep breaths', 'Practice self-compassion', or 'Celebrate small wins'. It activates most strongly on the terse, template-like phrasing itself—often just the imperative verb phrase plus a colon—rather than on any elaboration or personalized context that follows. It is largely agnostic to the specific self-care theme (breathing, gratitude, breaks, self-compassion) as long as the sentence has this generic advice-list cadence. It activates weakly or not at all on longer, discursive, or context-specific advice that explains reasoning, references a particular situation (e.g. 'your girlfriend', 'your dog'), or reflects on someone's feelings and actions rather than issuing a standalone generic self-care directive; numbered list markers alone ('2. **') without the self-care content activate it weakly or inconsistently.

title: Imperative 'Remember' as advice marker
description: This latent fires on the word 'Remember' used as a sentence-initial imperative introducing a piece of advice, reminder, or reassurance, typically in advice-giving or reflective response contexts (e.g. relationship or interpersonal guidance). It activates most strongly on the bare token 'Remember' (with or without a following comma or 'that'), essentially marking the onset of a didactic reminder clause, and activates more weakly on longer sentences where 'Remember that/,' introduces the actual advice content ('Remember that healing is a process', 'Remember, relationships are about growth...'). It would not activate on uses of 'remember' as a normal verb describing memory of a past event (e.g. 'I remember when...'), nor on other advice-giving constructions that don't use this specific imperative framing (like 'Consider...', 'Try to...', or declarative statements of fact).

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral token that begins an item in an enumerated or ordered list (e.g., '2.', '3. **', '4. **'), regardless of the content that follows. It activates most strongly on bare list numbers, especially '2', and more weakly on other small numerals (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) that head list entries, often followed by markdown bold markers. It does not activate on numbers used in other contexts, such as quantities, dates, measurements, or numerals embedded within prose, nor on list markers using letters or bullets instead of digits.

title: Short evaluative 'That's X' verdict
description: This latent fires on brief, formulaic sentences that open with the demonstrative 'That's' followed immediately by a short evaluative judgment (positive: 'great', 'a good sign', 'reasonable'; or negative: 'not okay', 'not cool', 'unacceptable') passing verdict on something just described, typically in advice-giving or interpersonal-conflict contexts. It activates most strongly on the terse, near-templatic exclamatory or declarative form 'That's [adjective/noun phrase].' with minimal elaboration, and less strongly on longer sentences that still contain this evaluative pattern embedded within more discursive text. It does NOT activate on longer explanatory or hedging sentences that discuss the same themes (validation, boundaries, reasonableness) without using the compact 'That's ___' construction, nor on sentences that analyze someone's situation or feelings in narrative form rather than issuing a short capsule verdict.

title: Generic invitation-to-elaborate prompt
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic conversational questions that invite the listener to share more, typically appearing as a closing or opening line in a supportive/therapeutic dialogue (e.g., 'Is there anything specific that's been on your mind?', 'Can you tell me more about what happened?', 'What do you think?'). It activates most strongly on generic, template-like prompts that lack specific content and could apply to almost any conversation, functioning as a content-free bid for the user to continue talking or disclose feelings. It activates more weakly on questions embedded in longer advice-giving text that carry substantive, situation-specific content (e.g., 'Is it a lack of sleep or exercise?', 'What kind of alternative gift were you thinking of?'), since these are tied to particular topics rather than being generic conversational scaffolding. It would not activate on declarative statements, explanations, or advice that do not take the form of an open invitational question.

title: Formulaic 'age-old dilemma' framing exclamation
description: This latent fires on short, stock exclamatory phrases that frame an upcoming topic as a familiar, recurring conflict or tension, typically of the form 'The [age-old/eternal] [dilemma/debate/struggle/conundrum]!' It activates most strongly on the bare template itself, especially the exact phrase 'The age-old dilemma!', and also fires (more weakly) on close variants like 'The eternal struggle!', 'The age-old debate!', or longer noun-phrase elaborations such as 'The age-old conundrum of X!' that still open with this rhetorical framing move. It does not activate on sentences that discuss dilemmas or conflicts substantively (e.g., explaining what the tension actually is, giving advice, or empathizing with a situation) unless they use this specific exclamatory 'age-old/eternal ___!' framing construction; plain empathetic openers like 'What a complex situation!' or advice sentences without this template contribute much less.

title: Affirming self-empowerment statements
description: This latent fires on generic, aphorism-like declarative sentences that affirm the value of confidence, self-belief, self-awareness, uniqueness, or other empowering personal qualities (e.g., 'Believing in oneself... can be incredibly empowering,' 'Everyone is unique in their own way'). These sentences share a templated structure: an abstract virtue or trait (confidence, self-awareness, kindness, friendliness, motivation) paired with a positive evaluative claim about its benefits ('is empowering,' 'is a powerful catalyst for success,' 'can bring joy'), often phrased as universal truths rather than advice directed at a specific person. It does not activate on situationally-specific advice, questions, empathetic validations of a particular person's feelings, or narrative/contextual statements about someone's concrete circumstances—even when those touch on similar themes like confidence or self-worth—because the latent tracks the generic, motivational-poster style affirmation rather than personalized counsel or descriptive narration.

title: Advice to have an honest conversation
description: This latent fires on the specific advice-giving template 'Have an open and honest conversation with [person] (about [topic]),' typically appearing as a recommended action step in relationship or interpersonal-conflict advice. It activates most strongly on the near-verbatim phrase itself, regardless of which family member, partner, or friend is named, and regardless of whether a specific topic (feelings, concerns, decision) is appended. It activates weakly or not at all on adjacent advice sentences that discuss communication, boundaries, or talking things through but do not use this exact 'open and honest conversation' phrasing (e.g., 'communicate openly with your roommates,' 'listen actively,' 'approach the conversation with empathy'), showing the latent is keyed to this specific formulaic recommendation rather than the general theme of communication advice.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral token that begins or marks an item in a numbered list (e.g., '5.', '7', '9'), typically at the start of a list entry, often followed by bold markdown formatting for a heading or label. It activates most strongly on bare digit tokens (with or without a trailing period) that serve as list enumerators in structured outputs like tips, steps, or options. It does not activate on prose sentences without list structure, on words that are not part of an enumerated sequence, or on numbers used as quantities/dates within regular sentences rather than as list markers.

title: Polite conversational requests to connect or shift topic
description: This latent fires on short, direct-address questions or brief statements proposing social interaction — asking to catch up, reach out, get someone's number, join in, take a break, or change the subject (e.g. 'Can we catch up soon?', 'Would you like to join us?', 'Can we talk about something else?'). It activates on quoted or scripted conversational openers/requests, often phrased as polite questions with modal verbs (Can, Could, Would) or as brief first-person statements of intent ('I should probably get going', 'I've been thinking about you'). It is strongest on the actual interpersonal utterance itself rather than on third-person advice, analysis, or explanation about communication; sentences that describe or coach how to communicate (e.g. 'Use "I" statements', 'You could say something like...') or that discuss feelings/relationship dynamics analytically do not trigger it as strongly, since the latent responds to the direct conversational request/offer form rather than meta-commentary about it.
